standards.name: MIRAGE Sample Preparation Guidelines (v1.0)
standards.abstract: These guidelines address sample preparation for glycomics research, covering generation, purification and modification of samples derived from biological or synthetic material. The recording/data modality is protocol and metadata reporting for glycomics experiments (supporting reproducible datasets and downstream analytical reporting, including mass-spectrometric workflows). The MIRAGE Sample Preparation Guidelines v1.0 were produced by the MIRAGE initiative (authors listed on the Beilstein/MIRAGE pages) and published in Glycobiology (2016). They provide community-agreed reporting guidance intended to standardize how sample origin, processing and defined sample identifiers are recorded so that datasets are understandable and reproducible.

classification.rationale: The source material is prose guidance listing aspects and reporting requirements (e.g. 'Following aspects are covered'), not a field-level table or an ordered workflow. Items are instructions/areas to report rather than concrete typed metadata fields, so the source is best represented as principles.

principles.principle: Guideline scope: include all aspects of sample generation, purification and modification from biological and/or synthetic material.
principles.evidence: The sample preparation guidelines are designed to include all aspects of sample generation, purification and modification from biological and/or synthetic material.

principles.principle: Report sample origin, including general information and whether material is biologically or chemically derived and a description of the starting material.
principles.evidence:
Following aspects are covered
Sample Origin: General information, Biologically derived material, Chemically derived material, Description of starting material

principles.principle: Report sample processing steps, specifically isolation (enzymatic and/or chemical treatment), modification (enzymatic and/or chemical modifications), and purification steps.
principles.evidence: Sample processing: (1) isolation: enzymatic and/or chemical treatment; (2) modification: Enzymatic and/or chemical modifications; (3) purification: steps

principles.principle: Provide a defined sample name (an identifier for the processed/defined sample).
principles.evidence: Defined sample: sample name

principles.principle: Use these guidelines to improve recording of experimental protocols and to support understandable and reproducible glycomics datasets; serve as a common basis for further MIRAGE reporting guidelines and to keep data-analysis requirements short and consistent.
principles.evidence:
Fundamentally, the application of MIRAGE sample preparation guidelines will lead to improved recording of experimental protocols and reporting of understandable and reproducible glycomics datasets.
In addition, these guidelines are considered as a common basis for any further MIRAGE reporting guidelines in order to keep the requirements for data analysis short and consistent.

standards.notes: Published as: Struwe et al., Glycobiology, 2016, 26(9):907-910. DOI: 10.1093/glycob/cww082. The source material is the MIRAGE (Minimum Information Required for A Glycomics Experiment) sample preparation guideline v1.0, available in PDF from the Beilstein/MIRAGE site.

standards.name: MIRAGE Mass Spectrometric Analysis Guidelines (glycomics & glycoproteomics)
standards.abstract: These guidelines describe reporting requirements for mass spectrometry experiments that identify and characterize glycans and glycoproteins. The research objects are glycomics and glycoproteomics experimental datasets (raw MS, processed peak lists, search results) acquired under typical LC‑MS, MALDI, or other MS workflows; the recorded modalities are raw instrument files, processed peak lists and associated metadata (software, parameters, databases, search settings). The MIRAGE MS guidelines are maintained by the MIRAGE initiative (hosted by/affiliated with the Beilstein-Institut group and international glycoscience experts) and were published as a versioned guideline (original MIAPE-based version 2013 and updated implementation 2025). They address the problem of incomplete and non-standardized reporting of MS-based glycomics/glycoproteomics results by prescribing concrete metadata items (data stamp, contact, instrument and source parameters, data locations, processing and search parameters, databases and thresholds) and recommended types/formats for those items to improve reproducibility and data sharing.

classification.rationale: The source material presents an explicit parameter-by-parameter checklist with an associated "Type of expected" column (e.g., 'Standard date', 'Short free text', 'URL, dataset', 'Number'), i.e. a genuine metadata table listing named fields and expected formats rather than only prose guidance. Therefore this standard is best represented as a table.

standards.name: MIRAGE Glycan Microarray Analysis Guidelines (v1.0)
standards.abstract: These guidelines cover reporting for glycan microarray (glycan array) experiments in which a glycan-binding sample (proteins, organisms, aptamers, etc.) is tested against an array of glycans printed on a solid surface and read by fluorescence scanning. The recording/data modalities include image-level raw scanner files (TIFF), quantified scanner output files (e.g. gpr), and processed numerical data linked to glycan identities. Published by the MIRAGE initiative (doi:10.3762/mirage.3; Version 1.0, 22 June 2016), the document defines minimal information required to make glycan array results interpretable: eight numbered reporting areas (Sample, Glycan library, Printing surface, Arrayer/printer, Array map/layout and QC, Detector and data processing, Data presentation, and Interpretation/conclusions). A supplementary reporting template is provided to assist authors in composing a supplementary table for manuscripts.

classification.rationale: The core document is prose guidance with numbered sections that list the minimal information to report (instructions such as 'The Sample description should include...'), i.e. a checklist-style set of reporting requirements rather than a formal metadata table with typed fields. Although a supplementary template (table) is provided, the standard itself is organized as principles/guidelines.

principles.principle: Minimal-scope guidance
principles.evidence: These guidelines were drafted to be intentionally minimal and apply only to information required for generating interpretable data from a glycan array experiment.

principles.principle: Levels of data to retain and report
principles.evidence: Similar to DNA microarray experiment, there are three levels of data relevant to a glycan microarray experiment: Level 1: Raw data (original TIFF image from array scanner) Level 2: Quantified numerical data output file (e.g. proscan or gpr) from scanner software Level 3: Processed data (after association with glycan identities, averaging of replicates with appropriate statistics, data selection procedures, filtering and sorting, etc.) The present MIRAGE guidelines suggest that only ‘Level 3’ data need be presented in published papers but also suggest that ‘Level 1’ and ‘Level 2’ data be retained by researchers so that it be available when suitable databases and processing software become accessible and that deeper data comparison and mining can be undertaken where worthwhile.

principles.principle: Report Sample (Glycan Binding Sample) details
principles.evidence: The Sample description should include an appropriate name, previous references, public database IDs (if available), its origin (synthetic, natural, or recombinant), and its source including vendor or method of preparation.

principles.principle: For protein samples describe purity and modifications
principles.evidence: For proteins, a statement of purity is required and may represent a quantitative or qualitative description; i.e., % purity based on a specific assay (quantitative) or a component of a mixture such as a polyclonal antibody in a serum sample (qualitative). Fusion constructs for recombinant proteins for the purpose of detecting should also be described. If sample is directly labelled, describe the method and reagents. Sample modifications (including sources) used for chemical labeling of the Sample, e.g. fluorescein, biotin, etc.

principles.principle: Report Glycan library composition and identity
principles.evidence: The minimal information regarding the glycan library should include: For mono- and oligosaccharides, the structure of each glycan, i.e. the sequence, linkage and anomeric configuration of each. When possible, accession numbers assigned by an authoritative informatics resource, such as the GlyTouCan glycan structure registry (https://glytoucan.org/) should be included.

principles.principle: Provide information on glycan purity, source and modifications
principles.evidence: The purity of each glycan should be indicated [MIRAGE Sample Preparations Guidelines (doi:10.3762/mirage.1) are recommended]. Sources/references of glycans should be specified. Methods/references for functionalization or derivatization of glycans, including the structures of linkers should be described. Any effects on the glycan structure; i.e., reductive amination of reducing monosaccharide, should be indicated. The purity of each glycan derivative should be indicated.

principles.principle: Report Printing surface details
principles.evidence: As the utility of the data generated from a glycan array analysis will be related to the quality of the printed array, minimal information regarding a surface on which the array is printed should include: What type of surface is being used; i.e., microscope-glass slide, microtiter plate or other format.

principles.principle: Report immobilization chemistry and handling of glycan derivatives
principles.evidence: Describe the non-covalent immobilization method; e.g. adsorption of lipid-linked glycans to nitrocellulose, or neoglycoprotein conjugates to polystyrene, nitrocellulose, etc. Describe any specific handling of the glycan derivatives required prior to sample deposition, e.g. formulation by adding carrier reagents. Describe the chemistry on the slide surface that enables the covalent immobilization of the glycan samples; e.g. NHS-ester or epoxide for amine functional groups, maleimide for sulfhydryl functional group.

principles.evidence:

principles.evidence:

principles.evidence: The present MIRAGE guidelines suggest that only ‘Level 3’ data need be presented in published papers but also suggest that ‘Level 1’ and ‘Level 2’ data be retained by researchers so that it be available when suitable databases and processing software become accessible and that deeper data comparison and mining can be undertaken where worthwhile.

standards.notes: The MIRAGE package also provides a supplementary reporting template (Supplementary Glycan Microarray Information Template) that lists the specific reporting items in table form; however the canonical standard text is prose guidance (checklist/principles). The template can be used by authors to create a Supplementary Table for publications.

standards.name: MIRAGE Liquid Chromatography Analysis Guidelines (v1.0)
standards.abstract: These guidelines cover metadata for liquid chromatography (LC) experiments used in glycomics, describing what should be reported about samples, instrumentation, chromatographic conditions, detection and data annotation. The recording modality is experimental LC runs and their outputs (chromatogram traces, fractions, and derived annotations), often coupled to MS or other detectors. The document is the MIRAGE LC Guidelines (Version 1.0, 1 March 2018; doi:10.3762/mirage.4), published as part of the MIRAGE initiative; it defines minimal and recommended descriptive fields to ensure reproducibility and re-use of LC data in glycomics. The scope covers general dataset descriptors, equipment and column specifications, mobile phase and run properties, pre/post-run processes, detection settings, fraction collection, data annotation, and exoglycosidase treatment metadata.

classification.rationale: The source is presented as a structured list of named metadata fields (e.g. 'Manufacturer', 'Model', 'Time stamp', 'Flow Rate', etc.) with definitions and expected content for each item. Each entry corresponds to an independently meaningful metadata field rather than procedural instructions, matching the definition of a Metadata Table.

standards.name: MIRAGE NMR Glycan Recognition Guidelines (v1.0)
standards.abstract: These guidelines cover reporting of NMR experiments and data used to characterize glycan recognition by receptors (proteins such as lectins and antibodies, organisms, cells, or synthetic glycan-binding molecules). The recording modality is NMR spectroscopy (1D/2D/3D experiments including 1H, 13C, 15N; STD; tr-NOESY; HSQC; WaterLOGSY; etc.) together with associated processed spectra, tables and figures. The MIRAGE NMR Glycan Recognition Guidelines (Version 1.0, 21 Sep 2020) are published as part of the MIRAGE initiative (doi:10.3762/mirage.5) to provide a comprehensive checklist of items to include in manuscripts or supplementary material so that glycan–receptor NMR binding experiments are reported consistently and reproducibly. The document lists sample descriptions, spectrometer and processing details, NMR-specific parameters to report, how data should be presented, and interpretation/conclusions to be stated.

classification.rationale: The source is a set of reporting guidelines presented as headings and checklist-like prose items (instructions about what to report), not a machine-formatted metadata table nor a procedural DAG. Items are wording of WHAT to report (e.g., 'Glycan sequence', 'Describe specific parameters'), so the structure is best represented as principles (reporting requirements) rather than a table of typed fields.

standards.name: MIRAGE Capillary Electrophoresis Guidelines (v1.0)
standards.abstract: These guidelines cover reporting for capillary electrophoresis (CE) experiments applied to glycomics/glycoprofiling (e.g., xCGE-LIF), where the recorded data are electropherograms and associated instrument/control files (e.g., .ab1, .fsa) and metadata about samples, reagents, capillaries and run conditions. The MIRAGE CE Guidelines (Version 1.0) were published by the MIRAGE consortium in Glycobiology (doi:10.1093/glycob/cwac021) and updated in 2021; they specify the minimum metadata to report CE experiments to ensure reproducibility and interpretability. The document enumerates concrete metadata fields (date stamp, responsible contact, experiment mode/aim, sample identification and solutions, instruments, software and capillary details, type/level of analysis, run steps and descriptors, and calibration/standards) and provides recommended formats (e.g., date format 'YYYY-MM-DD'), examples and references to complementary MIRAGE sample/MS guidelines.

classification.rationale: The source presents a structured checklist of named metadata items, many with explicit required formats or component subfields (e.g., Date stamp with 'YYYY-MM-DD', Responsible person listing Name/Postal address/Email/ORCID, capillary dimensions with specified units). This is a field-level metadata specification rather than prose guidance-only, so it is best represented as a MetadataTable.

standards.name: MIRAGE Lectin Microarray Analysis Guidelines (v1.0)
standards.abstract: This guideline covers reporting standards for lectin microarray experiments that profile glycan-containing samples (e.g., glycans, glycoproteins, cell lysates, cells, glycopeptides). The recording modality is primarily fluorescence microarray binding data (scanner images and quantified spot intensities) together with metadata about samples, lectin libraries, array fabrication, detection instruments, and data processing. The MIRAGE Lectin Microarray Guidelines (v1.0), published April 10, 2023 (DOI: 10.3762/mirage.8) and authored by Tateno et al., provides a structured checklist/template and explanatory text to standardize what experimental and processing details should be reported so results are interpretable and reusable. It is maintained as part of the MIRAGE initiative and addresses scope from sample description and preparation, through lectin library and array production, to detector/settings, image analysis, data processing/statistics, presentation, and data location.

classification.rationale: The source provides a multi-section reporting template and explicit table-like fields (a Supplementary Information template with named rows such as 'Description of Sample', 'Sample preparation protocol', 'Instrument settings', etc.). This is a metadata template with concrete named fields intended to be completed, i.e. a table, rather than merely prose guidance or an ordered workflow.

sample.assay_protocol.name: Assay protocol
sample.assay_protocol.descr: Protocol used for microarray binding analysis: sample concentration, composition of solutions, blocking/binding/washing times and temperatures, secondary reagents, and pre-complexing details (ratios, times, temperatures) if applicable.
sample.assay_protocol.evidence: Assay protocol The protocol used for microarray binding analysis of the sample. Describe the sample concentration used (and that of reference if added), the composition of solutions, time and temperature used for blocking (preventing nonspecific binding), binding, and washing, as well as the application of secondary reagent(s) required for the analyses. If the sample is pre-complexed with secondary detection reagents before adding to the array (e.g. anti-His antibody with his-tagged sample), give the ratio of reactants and pre-complexing time and temperature.

detector.instrument_settings.name: Instrument settings
detector.instrument_settings.descr: Scanner settings and evidence that signals are within linear detection range (scanning resolution, laser channel, PMT, scan power) and resolution adequacy.
detector.instrument_settings.evidence: Instrument settings The intensities of signals generated from sample binding to individual lectins are a reflection of affinities or avidities of the interactions. Indicate whether the scanner settings (scanning resolution, laser channel, PMT, and scan power) are such that signals are in a linear range of the scanner’s detector (no ‘saturation of signals’) and whether the scanning resolution is adequate for the sizes of sample spots.

data.processing_and_statistical_analysis.name: Data processing and statistical analysis
data.processing_and_statistical_analysis.descr: Details of how microarray binding results are generated and calculated: software, normalization, data selection, handling of replicates, transformation algorithms, scaling, and statistical methods.
data.processing_and_statistical_analysis.evidence: Data processing and statistical analysis Provide details of how data in the table of microarray binding results are generated and calculated, i.e., specific software, normalization method, data selection procedures, and parameters, statistical analysis (including how the data from replicates on the array were handled in the statistical method), transformation algorithm and scaling parameters.

raw_full_info.source_fragment: Data processing and statistical analysis Provide details of how data in the table of microarray binding results are generated and calculated, i.e., specific software, normalization method, data selection procedures, and parameters, statistical analysis (including how the data from replicates on the array were handled in the statistical method), transformation algorithm and scaling parameters.

data.presentation.interpretation.name: Data presentation and interpretation
data.presentation.interpretation.descr: Report software/algorithms used for interpretation (e.g., motif analysis): name, version, algorithm, derived data; or describe methods/criteria for selecting binders/non-binders if no algorithm used.
data.presentation.interpretation.evidence: Data presentation and interpretation If software or algorithms are used to interpret processed data, e.g. for motif analysis, information or references to the software used, software version, name of the algorithm, and derived data (if available) should be included. If software or algorithms are not used, methods or criteria used for selecting binders/non-binders should be described.
